HostDiscoveryRequest.description:
Host Discovery — Phase 1.

`pipeline_mode` tells the backend which pipeline this scan belongs to:
  "basic"              → only Host Discovery will run; scan is immediately marked complete.
  "asset"              → Host Discovery then Asset Discovery; scan stays 'running' after host discovery.
  "vulnerability_audit" → Full pipeline; scan stays 'running' until vulnerability audit.

`phases` is the authoritative list from the frontend (informational / audit).

`discovery_intensity` controls Asset Discovery Phase 1 strategy (asset pipeline only):
  "light"  → FAST profile only — fastest, may miss firewalled/restricted hosts.
  "normal" → FAST first, BALANCED fallback only for still-inactive IPs (default).
  "deep"   → Full BALANCED — maximum coverage, slower.
Ignored for basic and vulnerability_audit pipelines.

get.description:
Export the audit trail the caller can see, as CSV or PDF.

Taking a copy of the trail off the platform is itself an auditable event,
and it is written and **committed before the first byte is sent**. Two
reasons, and both are load-bearing:

* The chain insert holds a ``FOR UPDATE`` lock on the organisation's row in
  ``audit_chain_heads`` until commit. Streaming inside that transaction
  would hold it for the whole download — seconds to minutes on a slow
  client — and block every other audit write in the tenant meanwhile.
* ``get_db`` closes the request's session when the handler returns, which
  for a ``StreamingResponse`` is *before* the body is produced. An event
  written and not yet committed at that point is silently discarded.

The generator therefore opens its own read-only session. That is not the
second-session pattern ``core/audit.py`` prohibits: it writes nothing, and
the request's transaction is already committed when it starts, so there is
no lock for it to deadlock against.

delete.description:
End a tenancy by **archiving** the organisation. Nothing is deleted.

This route used to call ``db.delete(org)``. Thirty foreign keys reference
``organizations`` and every one of them is ``ON DELETE CASCADE``, so that
single statement destroyed the tenant's users, assets, scans, every
``compliance_*`` record including findings and evidence, and its entire
audit trail — irreversibly, with no undo, at exactly the moment an
offboarding is most likely to be disputed. For an audit and compliance
product that is the wrong default.

Archiving sets ``is_active = False`` as well as ``archived_at``, and that
flag is what actually denies access: it is already enforced in
``auth/jwt_handler.py`` (twice) and ``auth/router.py``. No new
authorisation code is introduced here, and therefore no new bypass surface.

``archived_at`` is deliberately not ``is_active`` on its own —
deactivation is a reversible suspension used for billing and temporary
lockout, archival is the end of the tenancy, and collapsing the two makes
a suspended tenant indistinguishable from a terminated one in the audit
trail.

Hard deletion is **not** available. When it is built it will be a separate,
explicitly named purge that first exports the trail and seals the tenant's
hash chain — the same delete-then-purge shape ``users`` already has.

The ``ON DELETE CASCADE`` relationships are left exactly as they were; this
route simply stops invoking them.

post.description:
Reverse an archival.

Member accounts are **not** silently reactivated. Archiving soft-deleted
them, and restoring an account is a decision about that person, not about
the tenancy — the same reason ``admin_users.restore_user`` leaves a
restored account inactive until someone explicitly reactivates it. A bulk
reactivation here would quietly re-enable an account that had been disabled
for its own reasons before the organisation was archived.

patch.description:
Update organization's active/inactive status.

Production Deactivation Flow:
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

DEACTIVATION (is_active: false):
  • All users in the organization lose access IMMEDIATELY
  • Existing sessions/tokens become invalid on next request
  • New login attempts are rejected with HTTP 403
  • Token refresh fails with HTTP 401
  • Individual user statuses remain UNCHANGED
  • Audit trail logs the deactivation event

REACTIVATION (is_active: true):
  • Users regain access without modification
  • No need to re-enable individual users
  • Existing tokens remain valid (if not expired)
  • Full reversal of deactivation state

Benefits:
  ✓ Instant access revocation without manual user modifications
  ✓ Reversible state - no data loss or extra cleanup
  ✓ Scalable - handles thousands of users in deactivated orgs
  ✓ Clean audit trail - org status change is primary audit event
  ✓ No token invalidation needed - checked on every request

Returns:
  Organization object with updated status

post.description:
Approve a pending account, allowing it to sign in.

Requires the mailbox to have been verified first. Approving an unverified
account would activate a login for an address nobody has demonstrated
control of, which is the whole failure this gate exists to prevent — so it
is refused rather than treated as an override.

The approved account keeps whatever role it was created with (`viewer` for
self-registration). Granting scan execution stays a separate, explicit act
through the role endpoint, so approval never silently confers it.

`allowlist_domain` is the second, wider decision and defaults to False.
Without it, approving a flagged account clears that one account and leaves
the domain exactly as it was — so admitting a colleague whose employer got
caught by an over-eager blocklist does not quietly open the door to every
address at a throwaway service.

patch.description:

Rules:
  - Only superadmins can move users across organizations.
  - You cannot move yourself.
  - The target organization must exist and be active.
  - All active refresh token sessions are revoked immediately
    so the user's next login picks up the new org context cleanly.

Example:

post.description:
Trigger a live NVD 2.0 sync into the application vulnerability catalogue.
Runs asynchronously in the background.

``days_back`` is the mode selector, and deliberately so. It used to be a
plain int with a default of 90 that the sync read and then discarded,
because the stored checkpoint overrode it on every deployment that had ever
synced — an operator could ask for a year of history, receive a 202, and get
the last few hours. Presence now means "backfill this window"; absence means
"carry on from the checkpoint".

parameters.description: Historical lookback in days. Omit to run the normal incremental sync, which resumes from the stored checkpoint. Supply a value to backfill exactly that many days: the checkpoint is then ignored and never advanced, so a backfill cannot move the incremental frontier past anything it failed to retrieve.

Report whether an email address can be used to register.

Deliberately does *not* answer "does this account exist". A taken address
and a free one both return available=true, and the collision surfaces at
submit time as a generic failure. Live "already registered" feedback on a
signup form is a convenience for the person typing and a bulk account
oracle for everyone else, and only one of those two is worth having.

The endpoint is kept so the frontend contract does not break, and it still
rejects syntactically invalid input, which is what the field actually needs
in order to give useful feedback.

It *does* now answer about the domain. A verdict of "this is a disposable
mail service" says nothing about whether an account exists — it is a fact
about the domain, identical for every caller — so surfacing it costs no
privacy and saves the person filling in the form from completing a signup
that is going to be refused at submit.

Check whether a username is free.

This is an existence oracle, so it is only reachable while self-service
registration is enabled — the signup form is the sole legitimate caller.
It answers about usernames only. It previously also matched the query
against the *email* column, which let anyone confirm whether a given email
address held an account by passing it here, and confirm it from the
username endpoint too. Usernames are semi-public within a tenant; email
addresses are not.

Create a new, inert account and email a verification link.

What changed and why
────────────────────
This endpoint used to create the account and return access + refresh
tokens in the same response, placing the user in a self-service
organisation with the `analyst` role. In this product `analyst` carries
scans:execute — so anyone who could reach this route could issue
themselves a working credential and point Nmap, Scapy and Nuclei at the
network from a worker running with raw-socket privileges on the host.

Registration now yields nothing usable:

  * the route only exists when ALLOW_SELF_REGISTRATION is on (default off,
    because POST /admin/users is the supported onboarding path),
  * no tokens are returned — 202, not 201, because the account is pending,
  * the account is created is_verified=False, is_active=False,
    approved_at=NULL and cannot log in until *both* the mailbox is
    confirmed and an administrator approves it.

The response body is identical whether or not the address was already
registered, so this route cannot be used to enumerate accounts.

Re-send a verification link.

Always returns 200 with the same body, whether the address is unknown,
already verified, or genuinely pending — the response must not reveal
which. Rate-limited per client because this endpoint sends mail to an
address the caller chose, which makes it usable as a mail relay against a
third party if left open.

Resets the user's password using the secure token.
Validates token presence, expiration, updates the user's password,
invalidates all current user sessions, and revokes the token.

Anti-automation
───────────────
This endpoint carried no rate limit at all, which made it the one
unauthenticated write path in the API that could be driven without bound.
That is not primarily a token-guessing risk — the token is 32 random bytes
and `/auth/forgot-password` next door was already limited — it is that an
unbounded endpoint produces no signal. A script could submit for as long as
it liked and the only trace was a stream of 400s that nothing counted.

Two ceilings now, both per client IP: a burst limit above, and an hourly
cap on *failed* submissions below. Failures only, so a household or office
behind one NAT address resetting passwords legitimately is never affected
by its neighbours — you have to be getting it wrong to accumulate.

Exchange a service's signed client assertion for a 10-minute service token.

Form-encoded, as RFC 6749 §4.4 and RFC 7523 §2.2 specify:
`grant_type=client_credentials`,
`client_assertion_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer`,
`client_assertion=<JWT signed ES256 by the service's own key>`,
`scope=<space-separated scopes>` and, for a service granted more than one
tenant, `tenant=<organisation id>`.

Answers 401 `invalid_client` for any authentication failure, 400
`invalid_scope` or `invalid_request`, 403 for a tenant the service is not
granted, and 503 when the service registry or the replay store is
unavailable.
Generate a short-lived (60s) JWT ticket for WebSocket connections and PDF downloads.

Redeem an email-verification token.

Verification proves control of the mailbox at this moment. It proves
nothing about identity and, on its own, grants no access: the account
still needs `approved_at` before login succeeds (unless
SELF_REGISTRATION_AUTO_APPROVE is deliberately enabled).

Failures are uniform — expired, already-used, never-existed and
wrong-user tokens all return the same 400 — so the endpoint cannot be used
to probe which tokens exist.

put.description:
Update a compliance rule's verification parameters and severity levels.

**Superadmin only, despite the `compliance:manage_rules` dependency.**

`compliance_rules` has no `tenant_id`: it is a single global catalogue that
every tenant on the installation is scored against. `manage_rules` is held
by `org_admin` as well as `superadmin`, so before this check an
administrator of one tenant could rewrite `check_definition`, `severity` or
`severity_weight` on any of the catalogue's rules and silently change the
compliance posture reported to every other tenant — weakening a control so
their own org passes, or skewing everyone's score through the weights.

That is a cross-tenant integrity flaw rather than a data leak, which is why
it survived the org-scoping review: there is no `org_id` to filter on. The
fix is to gate the writer, not the query.

The role is checked here rather than by swapping the dependency so that
`manage_rules` keeps working for the tenant-scoped compliance routes that
legitimately use it.

post.description:
Assign, reassign or unassign remediation ownership, in bulk.

The owner must be a user **in the same organisation**. Without that check
a caller could name any user id in the installation and hand another
tenant's employee a finding they can neither see nor act on.

Findings the caller cannot see are silently absent from the result rather
than erroring: a bulk call across a stale selection should not fail
wholesale, and the response reports how many were actually changed.

Record a decision to carry the risk rather than fix it.

Its own permission, deliberately. ``findings:update`` moves work through
the queue; deciding the organisation will live with a critical finding is
a different authorisation, and without the split anyone who can edit a
finding could clear their overdue list by accepting everything on it.

A reason is required and an expiry is optional. An acceptance that expires
returns the finding to the remediation queue on beat; one that does not is
a legitimate decision for a permanent compensating control, and
``accepted_at`` records when it was taken either way so it can still be
found and reviewed.

get.description:
Every remediation event for this finding, oldest first.

Read from ``finding_remediation_events``, which nothing updates or
deletes. So a changed owner, a moved due date or a withdrawn acceptance is
answerable months later even though the finding row carries only the
current values.

post.description:
Append a remediation note.

The finding keeps the latest note in ``remediation_notes``, which the
existing findings API and the reports already read. The event trail keeps
every one, so replacing the note does not destroy what it said before.

patch.description:
Move a finding through the remediation workflow.

**``verified_fixed`` is refused here and that is the point of the phase.**
The human transition table has no edge into it; a caller asking for it
gets a 400 saying a subsequent scan has to establish it, and pointing at
``pending_verification`` — which is the claim a person is actually in a
position to make.

``risk_accepted`` is refused too, but for a different reason: it needs a
reason and an approver, so it has its own endpoint and its own permission.

post.description: Return an accepted finding to the remediation queue by hand.

get.description:
Findings past their due date, soonest-due first.

``total`` counts every overdue finding and is never truncated by ``limit``
— a bounded count is a wrong number, where a bounded list is a page.

Findings whose fix has been claimed and which are waiting for a scan.

This is the queue that makes the verification requirement operable: an
entry here is somebody's word that the work is done, and it stays here
until an assessment agrees.

put.description:
Set this organisation's remediation deadlines.

Stored in ``Organization.settings`` — JSONB, already carrying per-tenant
configuration, so this needs no table. A partial update **merges** over
the current values: an organisation changing only ``critical`` keeps its
other five deadlines, where a replace would silently remove them and
report thousands of findings as carrying no obligation.

Changing the policy does **not** retroactively move existing due dates.
They are recomputed on the next scan's sync, and the change is in the
audit trail — rewriting thousands of historical deadlines from a settings
edit would alter what a past report said was overdue.

get.description:
Counts by remediation state and SLA position.

**Two aggregate queries, never a loop over findings.** A per-finding SLA
computation over the 4,633 findings one Linux host produces would be the
N+1 the materialised ``sla_due_at`` column exists to prevent — and this is
the endpoint a dashboard calls on every load.

The overdue count deliberately excludes ``verified_fixed`` and
``risk_accepted``: nothing further is owed on either, and reporting them
as late would bury the ones that are.

Export one scan's assessment results as a workbook, a CSV or JSON.

**What the export represents.** The benchmark verdicts are the per-check
results the Phase 3 engine produced during this scan and stored, read back
unchanged. Nothing is re-evaluated at export time, so a control that was not
assessed, could not be assessed, or does not apply is never rendered as
passed or failed — the six states stay six states. The scan's own immutable
GAP-12 policy snapshot travels on every row, so a reader can tell what was
in scope; the *current* policy row is deliberately not consulted, because
the policy may since have been edited and that changes nothing about what
this scan did.

**Filters narrow, never widen.** A framework the scan's policy excluded
cannot be named back into the export, because the rest of that framework was
never assessed and a partial score reads as a complete one.

**``csv`` needs one dataset.** A CSV is one table; ``dataset=all`` with
``fmt=csv`` is refused rather than silently exporting whichever table
happened to be first.

The vocabularies this build honours, read from the code that honours them.

A UI building a policy editor needs this, and hardcoding the lists there
means a family added by a later phase is unselectable until somebody

named frameworks are installed for this organisation is checked again at

and a validation cached at authoring time cannot know that.

delete.description:
Delete a policy.

Refused by default while a schedule references it. The foreign key is
``ON DELETE SET NULL``, so deleting anyway leaves the schedule running
under the request defaults — a silent broadening of what it assesses, which
is the thing this phase exists to prevent. ``force=true`` is the deliberate
way through, and the response names what it changed.

Completed scans are never affected: their configuration lives in their own
``options`` snapshot, which is why the snapshot is stored there rather than
as a foreign key to this table.

parameters.name: force

schema.description: Delete even though schedules reference this policy
schema.title: Force

post.description:
Switch a policy off without retiring it.

Disabling is deliberately **not** silent for anything pointing at it: the
response names the schedules that will now fail to dispatch. A schedule
running unnoticed under the request defaults because its policy was
disabled would assess something other than what was authorised, which is
exactly what this phase exists to stop.

Move a policy through draft → active → archived.

Archiving is this product's soft delete for a policy, and it is what an
operator should reach for: the row survives, so a completed scan's snapshot
can still be matched against a policy a reader can look up, while nothing
new can start under it.

get.description:
What depends on this policy: schedules now, and how many scans have run.

``scan_count`` counts scans whose *snapshot* names this policy id, read
from ``scans.options``, not a join — the snapshot is the record and a scan
keeps it after the policy is deleted.

post.description:
Supersede a policy with a new version of the same family.

The old row is archived and points at the new one, so a scan that ran under
version 2 still resolves to a policy a reader can look up, while everything
new runs version 3. That is what the family/version pair is for, and it is
the shape ``CompliancePolicy`` already uses.

Schedules are **not** repointed automatically. A schedule is an
authorisation to scan unattended, and silently moving one onto a
configuration nobody reviewed is precisely the substitution this phase
refuses everywhere else. The response names them so an operator can.

get.description:
The stored credentials this organisation can attach to a schedule.

Deliberately served here rather than reusing ``GET /compliance/credentials``,
which is gated on ``compliance:read``. Choosing a credential for a
credentialed scan is a scanning task, and requiring a compliance permission
to do it would either lock out an analyst who has no compliance role or
push somebody into granting compliance access for the wrong reason.

Returns identifying fields only — no ``encrypted_password``, no
``encrypted_key_content``. This is a picker, not a credential export.

Declared above ``/{schedule_id}`` because FastAPI matches in declaration
order and would otherwise read "credentials" as a schedule id.

The IANA zones this server can resolve.

Served from the server rather than hardcoded in the UI so the list can
never claim a zone the scheduler would then fall back to UTC on.

delete.description:
Delete the schedule and its run history.

The scans it produced are **not** deleted: ``scan_schedule_runs.scan_id`` is
ON DELETE SET NULL from ``scans``, and the runs cascade from the schedule.
A scan is evidence of what was found on a network at a moment in time, and
removing a schedule is not a reason to destroy it.

post.description:
Dispatch this schedule immediately.

Deliberately does **not** move ``next_run_at``. Somebody testing a schedule
at 11:00 would otherwise cancel that night's real run, which is a
surprising cost for pressing a button labelled "Run Now".

Works on a disabled schedule too: "disabled" means the recurrence does not
fire by itself, not that the definition is unusable — and running one by
hand is how an operator confirms a fix before switching it back on.

The stream honours the same filters as GET /scans. Without that, a live

get.description:
What changed between this scan and a baseline.

Both scans are fetched through ``_get_scan_or_404``, so the organisation
scoping and the per-user visibility rule that govern every other scan route
govern this one too — a caller cannot compare against a scan they could not
read, and cannot reach another tenant's findings by naming its id.

``limit`` bounds the returned rows, never the counts: an estate with
thousands of findings on one host still gets accurate totals, and the list
is the sample. That split is deliberate — a truncated count would be a
wrong number rather than a short page.

get.description:
The assessment configuration this scan actually ran under.

Read from the scan's own immutable snapshot, **not** from the policy row it
names. That is the whole point: the policy may have been edited, versioned,
archived or deleted since, and none of that changes what this scan
assessed. A question an auditor asks about a scan has to be answerable from
the scan.

``recorded: false`` is a real answer for a scan that predates GAP-12, and
it is not turned into a default policy — inventing a configuration record
would put a claim in front of an auditor that nothing supports.

Tenant scoping is ``_get_scan_or_404``'s, the same lookup every other scan
route uses, so another organisation's scan answers 404 rather than
disclosing its configuration.

delete.description:
Sign out every session except the one making this request.

The control that matters when somebody suspects their account is being used
elsewhere: revoking sessions one at a time requires knowing which row is the
intruder, and the whole reason for reaching this screen is not knowing.

Revocation, not deletion. The rows stay with `revoked_at` set so the audit
trail keeps showing that these sessions existed and when they were ended —
deleting them would erase the evidence of the event being responded to.

If the caller cannot be identified (no refresh cookie), every session is
revoked including whatever the caller is using. That is the safe direction:
"I could not tell which one is yours" must not mean "so I left them all
running".

get.description:
List active sessions for the current user.

This product allows an account to be signed in on any number of devices at
once, which is a deliberate choice rather than an oversight — capping it
would push people into sharing one browser or logging each other out, and
neither makes anything safer. What that choice *requires* is that the owner
of an account can see where it is signed in and end any of those sessions,
which is what this endpoint and the two below are for.

Expired rows are filtered as well as revoked ones: a row past its
expires_at cannot be refreshed, so listing it would show a session that
does not exist and invite someone to revoke something already gone.

Serve the proof screenshot captured for a finding (Codex item 10), e.g. a
rendered XSS. The finding must belong to the scan, and the stored path must
resolve inside the scan's own evidence directory — a screenshot_path is
written by the scanner, but this refuses to serve anything that escapes the
evidence root, so a crafted path cannot read an arbitrary server file.

The discovered form inventory (Codex item 1) — first-class WebForm rows
with their inputs, file-upload and password flags.

The attack surface at parameter granularity (Phase 23b relational model):
every (endpoint, location, name) with its coverage — tested, by which
engines, or why it was skipped. Filterable by location, coverage status and
name, which the JSONB parameter blob and the report's coverage summary
cannot answer relationally. Includes an ``untested`` roll-up so a caller can
see, in one call, how much surface remains unassessed.

  - All findings with HTTP evidence
